title: Resource Hijacking: SMS Pumping
summary: SMS pumping is telecommunications fraud that abuses a victim's messaging spend rather than the victim's computers. The adversary first acquires blocks of phone numbers from carriers on revenue-sharing ranges, then drives the victim's messaging infrastructure to send large volumes of messages at those numbers, collecting a share of the carrier payout. The preferred entry point is any publicly reachable form that triggers a message, such as one-time password delivery or account verification, usually behind providers like Twilio, AWS Simple Notification Service, or Amazon Cognito. Defenders should not rely on volume alerts alone, because the traffic is well formed and arrives over valid interfaces; the telling signals are application side and include requests that use syntactically valid but unreachable or unusual country number ranges, high request rates per source address across many addresses, verification flows that are never completed, and message spending that departs from the normal join between signup volume and successful account activation.

beginner.definition: SMS pumping is fraud that abuses a company's text message service. The attacker sends many messages to phone numbers they control. The company pays for every message, and the attacker earns part of the money back.
beginner.whyItMatters: Sending a text message usually costs money. A large flood of messages creates a large bill in a short time. Your monthly message budget can be used up in hours, so real customers stop receiving their codes. Your messaging provider may limit or suspend your account while the problem is investigated. Customers see failed signups, which damages trust and slows your business.
howItWorks: The attacker first obtains many phone numbers from a phone company that pays for traffic.
They find public pages that send texts, such as a login or signup code form.
Automated tools then submit those forms again and again with their own numbers.
Each submission makes your system send a real text message through your provider.
The attacker collects a share of the carrier payment for the received messages.
Your provider bill grows and message quotas fill, slowing real customer signups.
beginner.example: Imagine your flat shares one phone contract that charges for every text message sent. A stranger learns your number and signs you up for thousands of free trial codes. Each code is posted to a premium line that pays the stranger a small fee. The messages look as if they came from you. The bill arrives in your name and the line is blocked for a while. SMS pumping works the same way against a company's messaging account.
takeaways: SMS pumping costs you money by making your own system send paid messages.
Detect it by watching signup behaviour and spending, not just message volume.
One-time password and verification forms are the usual abuse point.

objectives: Explain what SMS pumping is and how the attacker earns money from it.
Identify which public features are commonly abused to generate messages.
Describe the account and quota impacts a victim experiences during an attack.
List request level signals, such as uncompleted verification flows, that reveal fraud.
Explain why message volume alone is a weak detection signal.
Summarise the defensive controls that reduce messaging abuse risk.
